sections.label: Permits refused for foreign involvement
sections.summary: Permits may be refused for assemblies and processions where non-Singaporeans and non-Singaporean entities get involved towards political ends.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The second is to re-emphasise and make clear what has always been our position, that permits may be refused for assemblies and processions where non-Singaporeans and non-Singaporean entities get involved towards political ends.

sections.label: Minister designates special events
sections.summary: Section 21 of the Act allows the Minister for Home Affairs to designate special events to ensure safety and security and avoid disruptions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Today, as it stands now before the amendment, section 21 of the Act allows the Minister for Home Affairs to designate special events.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This is done to ensure the safety and security of the event, and to avoid disruptions to the event.

sections.label: Police powers to require measures
sections.summary: The Police currently work with organisers to voluntarily put in security measures, but the time has come to give the Police powers to require such measures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: What the Police do today is to work with event organisers to voluntarily put in the security measures and most organisers are cooperative.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But I think the time has come for us to go beyond that to give the Police the powers to require such measures.

sections.label: Informing Police and declaring events
sections.summary: Organisers expecting crowds beyond a certain size must inform the Police in advance, and the Police will declare large or higher-risk events as special events.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: First, we will require organisers of events where you expect beyond a certain crowd, beyond a certain size, to inform the Police in advance that you are expecting this sort of crowd.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Second, after the Police's assessment, the Police will then declare events with certain large crowds, or assessed to be at higher risk, as special events.

sections.label: Crowd thresholds for public private events
sections.summary: Public events expecting more than 5,000 persons and private events expecting more than 10,000 persons at any time are covered.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For public events, if we expect more than 5,000 persons at any time, and public events refer to events where any member of the public can attend, either by purchasing tickets or by freely entering the event area.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For private events, if we expect more than 10,000 persons at any time.

sections.label: 28 days advance notice
sections.summary: Based on event type and crowd thresholds, the Police intend to be told 28 days before the event.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Based on the type of events and the threshold of crowds, I talked about the Police having to be told a certain period beforehand, we intend it to be 28 days before the event.

sections.label: Police notification for large events
sections.summary: There is a legal requirement to notify the Police when a public event's crowd size is reasonably expected to exceed 5,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: If you do not notify the Police, that would be an offence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, there is a legal requirement to notify the Police when you reasonably expect the crowd size to be beyond 5,000 for a public event.

sections.label: Examples of special events
sections.summary: Past precedent events such as marathons, concerts, countdowns, the Shangri-La Dialogue and National Day Rally will be declared special events.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Some of these events, based on past precedent, could include, say, large-scale sporting events like the Standard Chartered Singapore Marathon, music concerts and celebrations like the Chinese New Year Countdown or the Marina Bay Singapore Countdown.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: High-profile events like the Shangri-La Dialogue or National Day Rally will also be declared as special events.

sections.label: Additional measures for higher-risk events
sections.summary: For events at higher risk of terror attack or public order incident, the Police could direct measures like armed APOs, body scans and bag checks.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For some events which are likely to be at a higher risk of a terror attack or a public order incident, the Police could direct additional measures, like armed Auxiliary Police Officers (APOs), full body scans, bag checks and measures against vehicle-borne threats.

sections.label: Non-compliance with written directions
sections.summary: Not complying with written directions under section 30 would be an offence, and the Commissioner is empowered to give effect to his directions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Again, not complying with the written directions given under section 30 would be an offence, and the Commissioner is allowed or will be empowered to do what is necessary to give effect to his written directions.

sections.label: Enhanced security special events
sections.summary: Clause 8 of the Bill enacts a new section 21A allowing the Minister for Home Affairs to declare enhanced security special events.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 8 of the Bill will also enact a new section 21A.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: That is to allow the Minister for Home Affairs to declare some special events as enhanced security special events.

sections.label: Increased security requirements for events
sections.summary: Security requirements are increased for events attracting crowds over 5,000 and/or with national or international prominence, giving powers for directions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Basically, we are increasing the security requirements for events which attract certain types of crowd more than 5,000 and/or with national or international prominence giving powers for directions.

sections.label: Foreigners and political assemblies
sections.summary: Clause 4 lets the Commissioner of Police refuse permits for assemblies directed towards a political end and organised by or involving non-Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: As to the basic philosophy, there can be no doubt that the Government's position has always been that foreigners and foreign entities should not import their politics into Singapore, nor should they interfere in our domestic politics, especially on issues of a political or controversial nature.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 4 of the Bill clarifies that the Commissioner of Police may refuse to grant a permit for a public assembly or procession, if he has reasonable grounds to believe that the proposed assembly or procession is directed towards a political end, and organised by, or involves the participation of non-Singaporean entities or non-Singapore Citizens.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In determining whether the proposed assembly or procession is "directed towards a political end", the Commissioner would have to consider if such activities would cover matters, regardless of whether in Singapore or elsewhere, that promote the interests of political parties or a group of persons organised for political objectives, or influencing or seeking to influence policies or decisions of any government, changes in the law, any election or referendum, public opinion on a matter of public controversy, or policies or decisions of persons performing public functions, or to promote or oppose political views or public conduct relating to activities that have become the subject of political debate.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: These are directed at foreigners and foreign entities. "Singapore entity" in the Bill includes entities, such as companies and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), which are incorporated or registered in Singapore and controlled by a majority of Singapore Citizens.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Singapore Citizens and entities can continue to apply for and be granted permits for assemblies and processions directed towards political ends, as long as none of the other grounds which already exist in the Public Order Act are there.

sections.label: Clarifying public controversy term
sections.summary: The amendment to section 7 would better clarify the term "public controversy".

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: First, under the amendment to section 7, it would be useful to better clarify the term "public controversy".

sections.label: Number of active security officers
sections.summary: There are around 43,000 active security officers in the industry today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Today, we have around 43,000 active security officers in the industry.

sections.label: Entry-level security officer training
sections.summary: Security officers today complete two Workforce Skills Qualifications modules at entry level before deployment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Today, our security officers go through two Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) modules at the entry-level before they can be deployed.

sections.label: Security officers progressive wage model
sections.summary: The industry has established a five-grade single-track Progressive Wage Model for security officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Today, the industry has established a five-grade single-track Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for security officers.

sections.label: Security technologist graduate pay
sections.summary: An ITE graduate can join as a security technologist paid at least $1,800, while a polytechnic graduate can start as a senior security technologist.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: An ITE graduate in this area can join as a security technologist and get paid at least $1,800 for his specialty skills, while a polytechnic graduate can start as a senior security technologist.

sections.label: Security technology and manpower procurement
sections.summary: The passage states that procuring security technology separately from manpower is not tenable and calls for raising security standards and training officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Today, most buyers procure security technology separately from security manpower and this is not tenable in the long run.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: We hope that beyond addressing our long-term manpower needs through the sector's ITM, we can also raise the overall security standards that Singapore must have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: We are in a region where terrorism activities fester.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The security of our nation is paramount and we must spare no effort to ensure that our security officers are well-trained, well-equipped and well-informed to carry out their duties effectively.

sections.label: Clause 3 Police Commissioner discretion
sections.summary: Clause 3 proposes new discretion for the Police Commissioner and Minister, including prescribing different numbers of individuals for different event classes.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If I was to look at section 6A of the present Act, clause 3 proposes fresh discretion in the hands of the Police Commissioner and with the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It suggests, amongst other things, that the Minister may prescribe different numbers of individuals for different classes of events.

sections.label: Clause 9(e) modifying written directions
sections.summary: Clause 9(e) suggests the Police Commissioner may modify written directions under sections 1 or 7 without affording an opportunity to be heard.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Next, Madam, I look at clause 9(e) which relates to section 37 of the present amendment Bill.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It suggests that the Police Commissioner may, without affording any opportunity to be heard, modify any written direction under section 1 or 7 of the proposed above-mentioned legislation.

sections.label: Clause 9(g) new sections 38A 38B
sections.summary: Clause 9(g) seeks to create new sections 38A and 38B, and asks whether costs would be imposed concurrently with existing criminal sanctions.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Clause 9(g) relates to section 38 of the present legislation and seeks to create a new 38A and 38B.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Would these costs be imposed concurrently with the current criminal sanctions provided in the present 38 of the Act in the event of non-compliance with the Commissioner's written direction?

sections.label: Clause 4 permit refusal political end
sections.summary: Clause 4 lets the Commissioner refuse a permit if an activity may be directed towards a political end involving non-Singapore entities or non-citizens.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under clause 4 of the proposed amendment, the Commissioner has the power to refuse a permit for public assembly or public procession, if he or she has reasonable ground for believing that the activity may be, I quote, "directed towards a political end and be organised by, or involve the participation of, any of the following persons: an entity that is not a Singapore entity; and an individual who is not a citizen of Singapore." The term "political end" has a very broad definition, as mentioned by the Minister just now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For instance, a public panel discussion on animal abuse, featuring Singaporeans and foreign experts, can be considered as "directed towards a political end".

sections.label: Broad political ends definition concerns
sections.summary: The passage questions whether the Commissioner should refuse assemblies based on propensity to cause public disorder rather than merely determining political ends.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If we say that the proposed amendment is to restrict the direct influence of foreign corporations on domestic politics, then such instances can be dealt with through measures, such as disclosure rules, which will not limit spaces for political discourse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Therefore, the Bill, with its very broad definition of "political ends", seems to indicate that any event involving a foreign element advocating for some form of political change, whether good or bad, can be rejected by the Commissioner.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Therefore, my question would be: how would the Commissioner decide to refuse the application of a particular public assembly?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Should it be assessed based on its propensity to cause public disorder and not just merely on determining if it has "political ends"?

sections.label: Foreign expertise access restriction
sections.summary: The question asks whether proposed POA amendments restricting foreign involvement will limit access to foreign expertise and knowledge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Will the proposed amendments to POA restrict our access to foreign expertise and knowledge, given its prohibition of foreign involvement?

sections.label: Commissioner decides political ends
sections.summary: The POA provision gives the Commissioner power to decide what he or she deems to be political, or having political ends.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The provision in POA is such that the Commissioner is given the power to decide what he or she deems to be political, in other words, have "political ends".

sections.label: Police role as law enforcers
sections.summary: The position holds power to decide for the POA, but the Police Force should be law enforcers, not interpreters of political intentions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is why the position is invested with the power to decide on that for the POA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, the role of our Police Force should be that of law enforcers, not interpreters of political intentions.

sections.label: No reasons for permit rejection
sections.summary: Under the POA, the Commissioner is not required to provide detailed reasons for rejecting a permit application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Furthermore, under POA, there is no requirement for the Commissioner to provide any detailed reasons for the rejection of a permit application.

sections.label: Closer scrutiny of Bill
sections.summary: The speaker believes closer scrutiny of the Bill is required given the amendments' problems and potential to undermine public confidence in Police impartiality.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given that the proposed amendments are problematic on numerous levels, as well as the potential of undermining public confidence and trust in the impartiality of our Police Force, I believe that a closer scrutiny of the Bill is required.

sections.label: Security measures for large events
sections.summary: The Bill requires organisers of public events expecting over 5,000 participants to consult Police on security measures, and the speaker asks several related questions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Bill will require organisers of public events which expect more than 5,000 participants to consult the Police on security measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Security measures would include deploying more security officers, bag checks and installing anti-vehicle barricades.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: What happens if an organiser decides to set the number at 4,999 instead of 5,000 or split the crowd into two at venues in close proximity to each other?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Will the 5,000 include organisers and performers and supporting staff because, at some events, in fact, the performers and the supporting staff added up together could be more than 5,000 together with the participants?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: As there are limited choices of venues which can hold 5,000 people, will the Ministry consider designating such areas so that permanent security installations and measures can be set up in these areas to leverage the economies of scale and help organisers reduce costs?

sections.label: Special notice for large events
sections.summary: New section 6A requires organisers to give special notice to the Commissioner if they expect more than the prescribed number of participants.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The new section 6A requires organisers to give special notice to the Commissioner if they expect more than the prescribed number of participants.

sections.label: Defining political end assemblies
sections.summary: New section 7(3)(f) defines an assembly or procession directed towards a political end as one influencing public opinion on a matter of public controversy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Next, the new section 7(3)(f) defines an assembly or procession "directed towards a political end" as one that influences or seeks to influence public opinion on a matter of "public controversy".

sections.label: Commissioner judges political permit denial
sections.summary: Section 7(2)(h) requires the Commissioner to judge whether a political procession or assembly should be denied a permit because of its political nature.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 7(2)(h) will also require the Commissioner to be the judge of whether a certain political procession or assembly should be denied a permit because of its political nature.

sections.label: Independent body and rejection reasons
sections.summary: It asks whether an independent body should make these decisions, and notes the Commissioner has no obligation to give reasons for rejecting a permit application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Again, should an independent body be set up instead to make these decisions?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Also, the Commissioner has no obligation to provide any reasons for the rejection of a permit application.

sections.label: Support for organisers' security costs
sections.summary: It asks whether the Ministry is considering support for organisers, especially civil society groups, who may not afford enhanced security measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Is the Ministry considering any form of support to organisers, especially civil society groups, who may not be able to afford enhanced security measures?

sections.label: Notifying Police of expected turnout
sections.summary: Organisers must notify the Police within the prescribed period and give their best assessment of expected crowd turnout, with no offence if due diligence was exercised.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: When you organise an event, the organisers will plan with a certain turnout in mind, and they will have to notify the Police within the prescribed period and to give their best assessment of what they reasonably expect the crowd turnout to be.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the crowd size has exceeded, but they had exercised due diligence in their assessment, then that will not be an offence, obviously.

sections.label: Under-reporting expected turnout offence
sections.summary: Deliberate under-reporting of expected turnout is an offence, as is failing to notify Police of a planned larger crowd.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng asked if organisers may deliberately under-report expected turnout to avoid being declared a "special event".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think I have made it clear: deliberate under-reporting will be an offence, and if the investigations reveal that the organisers planned for a much larger crowd size but failed to notify the Police, that will be an offence.

sections.label: Security costs recovered as civil debt
sections.summary: Costs the Commissioner or Police pay for security measures will be recovered as a civil debt.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the Commissioner or the Police put in those security measures and have to pay for it, then that, as I said, will be recovered as a civil debt.

sections.label: Organiser pays part of security costs
sections.summary: For very substantive events, the organiser fairly pays part of the cost of additional security measures due to expected crowd size.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Where it is a very substantive event, it is only fair that the event organiser pays a part of the cost for additional security measures that have to be implemented because of the expected crowd size, such as bag checking, barricades and so on.

sections.label: Training for licensed security officers
sections.summary: Licensed security officers must be trained to Security WSQ standards, and training providers must be accredited.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Licensed security officers will need to be trained before they can carry out specific tasks.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: For example, how do you do security screening for individuals?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will require the training to meet the standards of the Singapore WSQ System for Security (Security WSQ), and training providers will need to be accredited.

sections.label: Amendments concern foreign participation
sections.summary: The thrust of the amendments relates to foreign participation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The thrust of the amendments today relates to foreign participation.

sections.label: Political end and foreign participation
sections.summary: Focus is on (h), covering events directed towards a political end organised by or involving non-Singapore entities or non-citizens.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we need to focus on (h) and not have a broad general political speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if you look at (h), it says "it is directed towards a political end and to be organised by or involve the participation of any of the following persons: an entity that is not a Singapore entity or an individual who is not a citizen of Singapore." And sub-clause 3 then relates back to this − what "directed towards a political end" means.

sections.label: Foreigners advocating political causes
sections.summary: Foreigners must not take public space for granted to advocate a political cause in, relating to, or outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Foreigners must not take our public space for granted to advocate a political cause, whether in Singapore, relating to Singapore, or outside of Singapore.

sections.label: Foreign-financed foreign-participated protests
sections.summary: Foreign-financed, foreign-participated protests are a different ball game, and the current amendments keep to that philosophy and rule.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Foreign-financed, foreign-participated protests are a completely different ball game.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The current amendments keep to that philosophy and that rule.

sections.label: Discretion given to Commissioner of Police
sections.summary: Discretion is given to the Executive, the Commissioner of Police, which is why the word is "may", there since 2009.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What you would have to do is then give that discretion to the Executive, in this case, the Commissioner of Police.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is why the word is "may", and that word has been there since 2009.

sections.label: Broad definition of assemblies and marches
sections.summary: The definition is broad and can cover many aspects, so the Commissioner can assess public disorder, threats and foreign involvement.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are talking about people marching, public assemblies, advocating specific causes and change.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I agree that the way that the definition is, it is broad and it can cover many aspects.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, you can have the Commissioner looking at it and say "is this something that will cause public disorder; is that a threat; what sort of foreign involvement is this and how does it impact on us?

sections.label: Commissioner decides security measures
sections.summary: A simple, clean, neat, effective way gives power to the Commissioner to decide the best security measures, avoiding long bargaining sessions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What we do not want is a long bargaining session with the Commissioner where they say "I will put up barricades but I do not want to put Auxiliary Police Officers" and that sort of arguments.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A simple, clean, neat, effective way to give power to the Commissioner to decide what security measures he/she thinks is the best way to go.

sections.label: Foreign interference through key organisers
sections.summary: A key person whose influence shapes an event towards specific political ends indicates foreign interference, and NGOs are a favourite route for foreign agencies.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If he is a key person and he is going to be organising everything, and really, it is his influence that impacts on the way the event is organised, the panel is chosen, towards specific political ends, then I think there is foreign interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But there can be many other situations, and this is not intended to be illustrative.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And it will not come as a surprise to you that NGOs are a favourite route of foreign agencies to channel funds and pressure governments.

sections.label: Clause 4 targets foreign participation
sections.summary: Clause 4 is specifically targeted at foreign participation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Clause 4 specifically is targeted at foreign participation.

sections.label: Foreign participation assessed case by case
sections.summary: Success does not require foreign money or participation, and events with foreign speakers are assessed case by case.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Do not think that you can only do well by getting money from foreigners and getting foreign participation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now, that is quite separate from having a foreign speaker or two in panels, getting their expertise and, by and large, those sorts of activities, it is going to be assessed case by case what is the nature of the event, what is the issue at hand.

sections.label: Reasons against judicial decision
sections.summary: The speaker explains why it does not make sense to have this go to a judge.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Kok, let us follow this analysis through.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have explained why it does not make sense to have this go to a judge, in terms of what is a political end, in terms of what is the potential impact on society, in terms of whether there can be a public order incident, whether this is a particular case for foreigners to be involved, to be allowed to be involved, to be not allowed to be involved.

sections.label: Government will make decision
sections.summary: Their position is that they will make that decision and accept being wrong.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Our position is that we will make that decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If we are wrong, we will take it on the chin.

sections.label: Security measures and clause 4(2)(h)
sections.summary: Security measures were included, and clause 4(2)(h) covers events directed towards a political end involving non-Singapore entities or citizens.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If we did not do it, people will say, "Why did you not put in those security measures?" The second other major change, as I was speaking with you, is on events, and I read straight from clause 4(2)(h), "directed towards a political end and be organised by or involved a participation of any of the following persons, an entity that is not a Singapore entity or an individual that is not a Singapore Citizen" and then it goes on to talk about what is a political end.
